toc.title: We don't release shutdown, we climb out of it
When to allow, and when to move

blocks.p: Someone in my community asked a question about coming out of shutdown. She was welcoming the sympathetic flight or fight activation as it came back, and she was worried that by allowing her shutdown, she was actually reinforcing her stuck state of shutdown. It's a valid concern, and I think a lot of people would assume the same thing. So let's work through it.
If you're in a dorsal vagal shutdown, it can feel very empty. It can feel like a void. You can feel very alone, dark. You might feel disconnected from yourself, from reality. You're an empty vessel.

When you come out of shutdown, up the [Polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system), you go into your sympathetic state. As the sympathetic energy comes back into the system, it can fill you up. That could be the experience of the activation coming back into your body: going from a shutdown collapse to feeling full of energy, full of motivation, maybe playfulness, the potential to create, to produce. There's this potential sensation of fullness, of filling up.

So when we're in shutdown, we feel empty. As we climb the Polyvagal ladder, as we self-regulate, the sympathetic activation comes back into the body, and we're much more mobilized and capable of things like play and creativity.
She went on: "If a nervous system has learned very early on to default to shutdown, and this is not a state we are choosing, it is a default when threat is detected..."

I want to rephrase this a little. No one is choosing shutdown consciously. Our nervous system isn't choosing it either. It's a biological reaction. Metaphorically we could call it a choice, but it's not. It's just a shift based on the needs of survival.

If we're raised in an environment where we can't be safe, where we can't connect to safe others or those efforts are constantly rejected, an environment we can't run away from, and where aggression isn't going to work, then we'll likely exist in a predominant shutdown state. It's not a choice. It's just the way it is.
So when threat is detected later in life, we don't choose shutdown. We're already in shutdown, if we exist in a chronic state of shutdown, and the threat just reinforces it.

Now, if you're pretty well regulated, you have connections with safe others, and your needs are taken care of or you're taking care of them, you might exist in a state with more safety. Then if you get into real danger, like you're actually being attacked, you'll go through the ladder sequence: flight, then fight, and then shutdown at the bottom. You could enter shutdown that way. But that's for a system that's already self-regulated.

blocks.h: We don't release shutdown, we climb out of it

blocks.p: She said, "I'm thinking this conditioning needs to be resolved and not released in some way." And yes, she's right. We don't release shutdown. We release flight or fight activation, from flight or fight, and also from freeze.

We don't discharge shutdown. Instead, the immobilization eases up, or softens enough, that mobilization, the sympathetic energy, can come back into the system. Then we become more mobilized, and we can use that activation. We climb out of immobilization. We return to mobilization. Releasing doesn't fit for me.

Freeze is different. Freeze is a combination of shutdown plus flight or fight. It's not literally frozen, it's not ice, but the immobilization of shutdown locks in the mobilization of flight or fight. So in freeze, we can release the flight or fight activation, but first the immobilization of shutdown has to come off, so the freeze can thaw. Once that comes off, the flight or fight activation is more accessible and can be used for healthy mobilization.

She continued: the conditioning of being in shutdown needs to be resolved, "so the other states and options are available again, and can be gone to when more appropriate or stand a chance of success (when we can actually fight or flee/stand up for ourselves or walk away)."

Yes. You have to come out of shutdown in order to access the potential of flight or fight. That might mean using that activation to escape an actually dangerous situation, or to stand up for yourself and speak from empowerment. Shutdown doesn't lend itself to those whatsoever.
Then the heart of it: "I think I'm worrying that allowing shutdown feels like I could be reinforcing that state as my go-to."
No, that's not going to happen if you're allowing shutdown along with your safety state.

If you exist in a predominant shutdown state and you try to allow it on its own, you might get sucked further into it. You might lock yourself in a dark room and sleep. That's not the kind of allowing I'm talking about. When I say allow your state, I mean allowing from being grounded in your safety state. If you're grounded in safety, then you can allow the shutdown to be there.

Think of it as dysregulated shutdown versus regulated shutdown. If you're in your safety state, you'll have regulated shutdown, and it'll be felt as the mixed state of stillness. Shutdown plus safety equals stillness.

Stillness is the ability to be immobile, and maybe alone, in solitude, but you're okay with it. You're safe. You're not getting sucked into a void of depression, disconnection, and isolation. From stillness, you can be self-reflective. You can have curiosity. You can have self-compassion. That's way different from allowing a dysregulated shutdown.
Deb Dana put it this way on the podcast:

q: Stillness is the most complicated autonomic blend of states, because how do you come into quiet, into stillness, without stimulating shut down? It's a tricky thing to do, especially for people with a trauma history. Because stillness is a very vulnerable place and I have to really feel safe to come into stillness.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.p: So if you allowed, or got pulled into, a dysregulated shutdown, would that reinforce it? Yeah, it totally would. Absolutely. But allowing shutdown from safety is what I mean.

When we come out of shutdown, we come up into fight and flight activation, and fight is typically the first stop. But even before that, as you build up your safety capacity, your safety state, your connections to yourself and others in the present moment, you'll likely experience the mixed state of stillness. That's not fight. That's stillness. And that's what we want.

blocks.h: When to allow, and when to move

blocks.p: Her last question: "I'm struggling with when it would be appropriate to accept and allow my shutdown, and when some movement intended to bring sympathetic energy in would be the way to go."
From shutdown, the way to sympathetic is more likely to be a lack of movement. You can move, do whatever you want. But shutdown needs immobilization. Shutdown needs reduced stimulation.

ol: Arrange your environment for safety. Alter your environment to give yourself more cues of safety, both passive and active, that speak to your safety state while you're in shutdown. That probably means reduced stimulation: lower lighting, softer music, or quiet. Heavy metal and hip hop probably won't be the places to go for that.
Allow the immobilization from safety. If you can allow immobilization from safety, self-regulation might help the sympathetic system come back online.

Let movement start very small. As you move from shutdown into sympathetic flight or fight, mobility becomes more of an option. From shutdown, that might be very small movements, not much at all. It might just be reorienting to the environment with your eyes.

blocks.p: Someone in the community shared a really nice example of this. The prompt for the day was to use your senses to connect to the environment. They were on a train, and they mentioned being shut down, so they closed their eyes. Instead, they focused on the sensory experience of the fabric of the seat, and then the metal of the chair.

So they reduced their stimulation. They closed their eyes, and they focused on one sensory aspect. From there, they felt the need, or the readiness, to open their eyes and look outside, and they noticed the skyline, the line of the building tops. They felt more connected and appreciative, and realized, "I've never seen this. I've never experienced this, even though I've been on this train every day."
That's a small, wonderful example of allowing shutdown and then slowly starting to come out of it: a more expansive awareness, connecting further to the environment using another sense.

It's also a pretty good example of stillness. You're in your safety state, but immobile. You're connected to the environment and to your present moment sensory experience, and there's a feeling of expansiveness and novelty. That could easily build into more mobility coming back into the system, into flight or fight.

If you keep practicing like that, at some point, the next day or the day after, you might feel like breathing more into your chest. You might feel more energy coming into your system. You might feel ready to get up and start walking as part of a daily routine.

So we don't start in shutdown, mobilize, and then the sympathetic activity comes in. Instead, the sympathetic activity starts to come in a bit at a time, and we expand from there, connect to the environment differently, and start being more mobile.
She wrapped up: "I worry about sinking into that despair and reinforcing a nervous system imprint that isn't serving me."

It's a valid concern, especially from shutdown. From shutdown, we assume we're going to fail. We assume things won't go well, that we'll be stuck in this state forever, that our efforts will fail, double the stuckness, and reinforce the imprint.

But as long as you're prioritizing safety and then mindfully allowing your shutdown state, it doesn't have to be that way whatsoever. It would actually be the start of real self-regulation: combining safety plus shutdown, and existing in stillness.
